newsitem.title: UK: Leads say terms not set on S.Africa Yankee, Samurai.
newsitem.headline: Leads say terms not set on S.Africa Yankee, Samurai.

text.p: Merrill Lynch and Daiwa, chosen underwriters for South Africa's upcoming second Yankee and Samurai, said on Friday that the bonds' terms were still to be decided.

"Nothing has been determined," Merrill Lynch Yankee capital markets managing director Christian Schade said, adding "We look forward to working with South Africa commensurate with its goals of creating benchmarks and extending maturities."
Daiwa Europe co-head debt origination Vincent Purton said: "Its very early days, at the moment there is no decision on size, maturity or timing."
"In the next few days we'll put some meat on it but there has been no precise discussion yet and we would not want to be tied down to a particular maturity," he said.
But syndicate officials in London and New York said the country was expected to launch a $400 to $500 million 20-year Yankee bond.
Market price talk was a range of between 190 and 210 basis points over U.S. Treasury notes for a 20-year bond.
The size of the Yankee is expected to be consistent with the previous deal. In October last year, South Africa launched a $300 million 10-year Yankee via Merrill Lynch.
The bond was priced to yield 195 basis points over U.S. Treasury notes and was last trading tighter at around 160 b.p, traders said.

The Samurai issue is expected to have a maturity longer than its previous five-year deal, either at seven- or 10- years, traders said. South Africa launched its first Samurai in May 1995 -- a 30 billion yen five-year offering with a five percent coupon -- also via Daiwa. South Africa said market conditions would determine the terms, conditions and timing of the two transactions which will form part of the government's budgeted amount of about 4.0 billion rand to be borrowed in foreign markets in 1997/98 (April-March).

"In keeping with the foreign borrowing strategy adopted in 1996, the emphasis will be on extending the maturity profile of foreign currency denominated debt, whilst at the same time further reaching out to new investors," the department said in a statement.
The country is rated Baa3 by Moody's Investors Service and BB+ by Standard & Poor's.
